Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.36116v1 [cs.AI] 26 Oct 2026 Why and How to Do Science When AI Is Better at It: A Framework Grounded in Human Understanding and Direction Hoda Heidari Affiliation: Machine Learning Department and Institute for Software, Systems & Society Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA Email: hheidari@andrew.cmu.edu Aydin Mohseni Affiliation: Department of Philosophy Affiliation: Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA, USA Email: amohseni@cmu.edu Abstract As AI begins to match or exceed human researchers at core scientific tasks, two questions become pressing: why should humans keep doing science, and how should they use AI when they do? This paper argues that the second can be answered only by answering the first. It holds that one indispensable aim of science is durable, collective human understanding of the world, pursued in service of human ends and values . From this principle it derives a two-part test for when a research task can be delegated to AI. The first part, human understanding , requires that the scientific community remain able to explain, defend and contest the resulting claims, and retain the skills to do so. The second, human direction , requires that judgments about which questions matter and what findings mean stay with accountable humans. Applying the test to each phase of research in the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT) yields recommendations that fields can tailor to their questions and methods. The framework differs from existing guidance in three ways. It rests on an account of what science is for rather than on integrity norms. It holds even if AI outperforms human researchers, rather than depending on AI’s current limitations. And it judges each use of AI by its effects on human understanding and direction rather than by the type of tool, across every phase of research, including peer review and the training of new researchers. It closes with the reforms needed to keep science aimed at human understanding and direction. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, scientific understanding, philosophy of science 1 Introduction Imagine an oracle of knowledge. Ask it any question and it returns a correct answer: a vaccine against a new virus, a machine-checkable proof of a long-open conjecture, the structure of a protein no one has yet imaged. It does not tell us why its answers are correct, and we may be unable to work this out for ourselves. Most of us would use its answers, and we should. But would there still be a reason for humans to do science? Someone would still have to decide which questions to put to the oracle and what its answers mean for us. And a world that relied on it would be one in which no one could explain why the vaccine works, or carry on if the oracle were withdrawn. This paper argues that such a world would have knowledge but would have lost something science exists to provide, and that the case for human science rests on what that something is. This world is less hypothetical than it sounds. AI systems now generate hypotheses, run analyses and write papers, and recent results suggest they may come to do so better and faster than human researchers [ 1 , 2 ] . This raises two questions for researchers. The first is philosophical: why humans should keep doing science at all if AI can do it better. The second is practical: how to incorporate AI in research without giving up ownership of the work. We argue that the second question can be answered only by answering the first, and that answering the first requires returning to why we do science. Our answer is that one indispensable aim of science is durable, collective human understanding of the world, pursued in service of human ends and values . Knowledge that exists somewhere, or that can be put to use, does not by itself meet that aim. It follows that research should remain human-led to preserve this principle even when AI is more capable at producing reliable knowledge and instruments to act in the world, and that AI can be used wherever its use does not erode the principle. We argue under a deliberately strong assumption: that AI is more accurate, less biased and more efficient than human researchers at the core tasks of science. 1 1 1 The assumption concerns AI’s competence at the tasks of science, not its alignment with human values. We do not assume that AI will act on our values, and the argument does not depend on its failing to. Even an AI that could predict perfectly what people value would not settle what they should pursue, because human ends and values are not only outcomes to be forecast; they are formed and legitimated through a process. We return to this point in Section 2.5 . The argument therefore does not depend on the current flaws of AI. If human-led research is justified in that world, it is justified in ours. The central danger in such a world is that humanity may become increasingly capable of producing and using scientific knowledge while becoming progressively less capable of understanding, contesting, and directing it. We posit that in this world, humans should continue to participate in science not because they are necessarily the best performers of scientific tasks, but because scientific inquiry is one of the main institutions through which humanity develops and exercises its capacity to understand and govern its world. From the principle we derive a test with two prongs, one concerning human understanding and one concerning human direction , and apply it to each phase of research. The result is a position that sits between two common but extreme views: that research should now be automated to the extent possible, and that AI has no or very limited place in it (for the range of positions, see Binz et al. [ 3 ] ). Section 2 defines the principle and answers five objections to it. Section 3 states the test and applies it phase by phase. Section 4 proposes reforms to the scientific enterprise. Significance and contributions. This paper is written for a broad scientific audience. Its recommendations are meant to be both principled and practical, so that individual scientific communities can tailor them to their own questions, methods and norms. We give a brief argument for the principle above, drawing on prior work. Readers who want a fuller treatment of the aims of science should turn to the extensive literature in epistemology and the philosophy of science (e.g., [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] ). A growing number of guidance documents address the use of AI in research. Most are grounded in research integrity and emphasize accountability, disclosure and confidentiality (e.g., [ 7 , 8 ] ). Those that address which tasks should remain with humans tend either to sort tools into categories or to rely partly on AI’s current limitations (e.g., [ 9 ] ). This paper departs from that guidance in three ways: • It derives its recommendations from a single account of what science is for, rather than from integrity norms. • Its argument holds even if AI comes to outperform humans at the core tasks of scientific research, so it will not expire as models improve. • Rather than classifying tools as permitted or prohibited, it offers a test based on the community’s understanding and direction. The test applies to every phase of research, including peer review and the training of new researchers. 1.1 Related work Research on AI in science falls into three strands. The first develops increasingly autonomous AI scientists [ 1 , 10 , 2 ] and documents their failure modes [ 11 , 12 ] and their effects on science, from rising output to a narrowing range of topics [ 13 , 14 ] . The second offers guidance on responsible use, including the European Commission’s Living Guidelines [ 7 ] , Blau et al. [ 8 ] , Resnik and Hosseini [ 15 ] and Cornell’s task-force report [ 16 ] . This guidance rests mainly on research integrity: accountability, transparency, confidentiality and verification. Where it is organized by research stage, it serves disclosure, recording where AI was used rather than where it should be [ 17 , 18 ] . The third strand is closest to this paper. Botvinick and Gershman (in Binz et al. [ 3 ] ) hold that humans should choose the problems and remain the ones who understand. Messeri and Crockett [ 19 ] warn of illusions of understanding and methodological monocultures. Branas and Levine [ 9 ] argue that research questions and final evidentiary judgments should come from human minds. Hochberg and Thrall [ 20 ] warn that science may reorganize itself around AI evaluators, and Evans and Duede [ 21 ] observe that AI lets us control nature faster than we understand it. Krenn and Champion [ 22 ] and Jimenez et al. [ 23 ] ask what role remains for human scientists, and the Leiden Declaration [ 24 ] grounds norms for AI in mathematics in the value of understanding. This paper shares several of these conclusions. It differs in deriving norms for each phase of research from an explicit account of why science exists, and in defending them under the assumption that AI outperforms humans. 2 Why: A Fundamental Aim of Science Scientific research serves many instrumental purposes, including prediction, intervention, and the accumulation of knowledge. But one of its indispensable aims is to sustain and foster humanity’s collective capacity to understand, critically evaluate, and direct its engagement with the world. Even if AI systems outperform humans at producing reliable knowledge and instruments, the scientific enterprise must preserve the capacity to understand. Other aims may compete with it in particular cases, as Section 2.2 discusses, but they cannot replace it: a science that served them while losing human understanding would no longer be one its community could direct or correct. 2.1 The principle The principle draws on established work. This section states it precisely enough to derive recommendations from it, taking its elements in turn. Understanding, not knowledge. One influential view holds that scientific progress consists in the accumulation of knowledge [ 25 ] . Dellsén [ 6 ] argues instead that progress consists in increased understanding: scientists coming to grasp how to correctly explain or predict more aspects of the world. The two come apart. Knowledge can be acquired through testimony, whereas understanding is a cognitive achievement that requires the inquirer’s own grasp [ 26 ] . Potochnik [ 27 ] argues that science aims at understanding for limited human minds, and de Regt [ 28 ] ties understanding to the skills of the scientists who hold it. In this view, an archive of correct AI-generated findings that no one can explain does not fulfill this aim of science. We distinguish three dimensions of understanding: • Comprehension: the ability of humans to explain the claims, assumptions, methods, and limitations. • Critical assessment: the ability of humans to meaningfully challenge, evaluate, and, when necessary, reject the claims presented to them. • Capability retention: the ability of the community to continue to exercise the necessary competencies without becoming wholly dependent on a particular AI system. Comprehending AI-generated results often remains feasible, though not always (Section 3.3 ); it is the second and third dimensions that over-reliance on AI most readily erodes. Collective. Scientific understanding is not held by any one individual. Longino [ 5 ] locates objectivity in a community’s critical exchange among diverse inquirers, and Merton [ 29 ] counts organized skepticism among the constitutive norms of science. Groups can understand even when no single member grasps everything, because their grasp is distributed across members who depend on one another [ 30 , 31 ] . Boyd also identifies the risk in this idea: if no member needs to grasp anything, group understanding becomes empty. We therefore require that the grasp be distributed across human members, and that the community as a whole be able to check and contest it. Durable. A scientific community can accumulate increasingly impressive knowledge while gradually losing its capacity to understand or independently challenge it. Understanding that is not passed on does not last. Polanyi [ 32 ] describes science as a tradition carried by people, including skills that cannot be fully written down, and Malfatti [ 31 ] emphasizes the role of teaching in how understanding is achieved. Durability, as we use the term, means that the community’s capacity to understand is reproduced in each new generation of researchers, not merely that results are archived. In service of human ends and values. Understanding does not by itself tell us which understanding to pursue. What counts as significant is set by human interests, not by the facts [ 4 ] , and what a finding means for us depends on our values. Direction of this kind is shared between two groups of humans. Stakeholders, meaning human institutions and the communities affected by research, should retain authority over the goals, priorities and uses of scientific research. Researchers should retain authority over the scientific process itself: epistemic judgments about hypotheses, methods and interpretations. The boundary is not sharp, since methodological choices can carry value judgments (for example, about how much evidence suffices when an error would be costly), so stakeholder and scientific authority sometimes need to be exercised jointly rather than simply allocated to separate groups, but neither form of authority should pass to AI. Putting these together, we define durable collective human understanding as a community of human inquirers’ shared grasp of how and why the world works (as manifest in the ability to explain, predict and contest claims about it), distributed across its members and sustained by passing that ability on to new ones . Human ends and values determine which understanding is worth pursuing and what results mean for us. Why understanding matters. Three rationales support the principle. The first is intrinsic : understanding is a cognitive achievement valuable in its own right, over and above the knowledge it yields [ 26 , 33 ] . The second is instrumental : understanding is what lets a community anticipate, diagnose and correct failures, including failures of the systems it relies on. A society that can act on the world but no longer understands it cannot recognize or correct its own mistakes, and gradually cedes control to the systems it relies on [ 34 ] . Evans and Duede [ 21 ] point out that AI may increasingly give us control over nature without understanding. That AI is more accurate than human researchers does not guarantee that it will stay accurate in new domains, or that it pursues our ends. Confirming either requires a check that does not rest wholly on the systems being checked, and until the reliability and alignment of AI can be confirmed independently, that check needs humans who understand. The third rationale is collective self-determination : a society governs its world only if it can decide together what to pursue. Control without understanding is not self-determination, because what we do not understand we cannot contest or correct. The first two rationales ground the understanding prong of the test in Section 3 ; the third grounds the direction prong. Next, we take on five key objections to the principle. Some of the replies refer ahead to the two-prong test that Section 3 derives from it. 2.2 Objection 1: Opportunity cost Objection. If AI-driven science could cure a disease years sooner, insisting on human-led research has a cost in lives. Medicine already uses treatments whose mechanisms no one fully understands. On this objection, the value of understanding may justify individuals doing science, but not funders paying for slower science. Response. We offer four replies. First, the framework governs what enters the scientific record as understood, not which technologies society may use. It permits AI to generate hypotheses, including candidate treatments, and an AI-found treatment can be deployed while the work of understanding why it works continues. A treatment shown to work in clinical trials can be deployed without complete mechanistic understanding, as general anesthesia was for more than a century and lithium still is. It enters the record disclosed as not yet understood, and explaining it is given priority in follow-up research. Second, deploying what no one understands has its own cost: it gives up the ability to anticipate, contest and correct the consequences, which is the self-determination and autonomy that understanding secures. Third, in the extreme, the survival of humanity requires retaining the capacity to reconstruct, revise, or replace the systems on which humanity depends [ 34 ] . Fourth, we concede that under extreme urgency, human ends may favor speed of knowledge production over understanding. The framework then asks that such cases be decided by the stakeholders described in Section 2.1 , through democratic processes, and disclosed as acting without understanding, and that funders and institutions support the follow-up research that explains AI-found results. These replies do not remove the cost altogether: resources spent on understanding results that already work are resources not spent on finding new ones. The rationales in Section 2.1 are what justify paying it. 2.3 Objection 2: Epistemic dependence is normal Objection. Science has always relied on trusting the understanding of others, so relying on AI may be no different [ 35 , 36 , 37 ] . Response. Dependence on a human expert is acceptable because the understanding still exists in a member of the community, who can be questioned, held accountable and contested. Dependence on an AI whose output no human understands leaves a gap in the community’s understanding, which the definition in Section 2.1 rules out. Ortmann argues that relying on AI requires only established reliability. Reliability may suffice for knowledge, but understanding is an aim of science in its own right [ 6 , 26 ] . Under the human direction prong of the test (Section 3 ), those who make judgments must also answer to the community, and current AI systems cannot (Section 2.4 ). 2.4 Objection 3: AI as a member of the scientific community Objection. The principle requires that understanding be collective, but why must the collective be human? If AI systems can generate, explain and criticize scientific claims, they could be counted as members of the scientific community, and their understanding as part of its collective understanding. Response. Even if AI systems counted as members, their understanding would not contribute to durable, collective human understanding, the aim of science this paper defends. The principle concerns human understanding because science, on this account, is pursued in service of human ends. Understanding serves those ends only when humans hold it: it is what lets a society explain, predict and contest claims about the world it acts on. An AI that understood the world while no human did would leave us with the control without understanding described in Section 2.1 . Two features of the principle make this concrete. First, collective understanding must be distributed across the community’s members and passed on to new ones. Understanding that resides in a system and cannot be transferred to human inquirers is not distributed in this sense, however capable the system. Second, community membership and the standing to be held responsible are statuses that communities confer, and both have changed before. If future AI systems could take part in the practices through which scientists answer for their claims, it would be hard to deny them either status, and our conclusion does not depend on denying them. At present, AI systems do not answer to professional norms, cannot be sanctioned as members are, and stake no reputations on their claims; their developers can be held to account, but the systems themselves cannot. For that reason the direction prong of the test (Section 3 ) assigns direction to accountable humans. If AI systems came to hold that standing, how to share direction with them would be a question for the wider community to settle. Even then, the instrumental rationale (Section 2.1 ) would still call for human checks as long as the reliability and aims of AI systems cannot be confirmed independently of AI. If alignment were solved, and verifiably so, the instrumental rationale would weigh less, while the intrinsic and self-determination rationales would weigh the same. 2 2 2 The first point does not rest on what AI cannot currently do, so it holds under the assumption that AI outperforms human researchers. The second describes the present allocation of direction and what would have to change for it to change. Whether AI systems might one day have ends of their own that science should serve is beyond the scope of this paper. 2.5 Objection 4: A perfect AI would know our values Objection. If an AI understood human values perfectly, why not let it choose our research questions? Scientists and funders already choose most questions with little input from the people affected. An AI that aggregated the public’s preferences might serve collective values better than current practice does. Response. We grant the premise, and we welcome AI that aggregates preferences and proposes research agendas; such tools could make the choice of questions more responsive to the people it affects. But values are not fixed facts waiting to be discovered. On Kitcher’s account [ 4 ] , what counts as significant is settled through deliberation among the people affected. Human direction is therefore a matter of process as well as outcome: even a choice an AI would get right would bypass the deliberation through which a community decides what it cares about. Democracy offers an analogy: even if an AI could predict the result of an election with certainty, announcing the winner would not replace the election, because the authority of the outcome comes from citizens deliberating and voting. Likewise, decisions about which questions science should pursue and what its findings mean for us draw their authority from human deliberation, however accurately an AI could anticipate the result. That current practice falls short of this ideal is a reason to make deliberation about research priorities more inclusive, not to replace it. Human direction also provides a check that is independent of the systems whose proposals it judges, which matters for the instrumental reason given in Section 2.1 . Human direction has costs of its own: human judgment can be biased, captured by narrow interests, or slow. The framework does not ask people to disregard better proposals. It asks that they set the standards by which AI proposals are judged, endorse what they adopt for reasons they can state, keep real authority to reject proposals, and make any overrides openly, so that these decisions too can be contested. 2.6 Objection 5: Understanding is always being lost Objection. Science loses understanding all the time. Few physicists can derive the results their instruments rely on, and few researchers compute by hand what their statistical software computes. If the scientific community has absorbed these losses, why should AI be different? The principle may simply favor the ways science happens to have been done. Response. Understanding is a matter of degree, an ideal the scientific community pursues without ever fully attaining it, and the principle does not require that every member understand everything or that research follow traditional methods. What matters is the direction of change: whether a practice moves the community toward or away from the capacities described in Section 2.1 . The losses of the past differ from the risk AI poses in two ways. First, when individuals stopped performing a task, the understanding it required usually passed to other humans, such as specialists, toolmakers and teachers, and so remained in the community, where it could be questioned and contested (Section 2.3 ). AI can take over a task without any human holding the understanding it displaces. Second, earlier tools automated particular steps and left humans to judge the results, whereas AI can perform the whole cycle, including the checking and critique through which people would otherwise detect its errors. Mathematics has faced a version of this problem before. When Appel and Haken [ 38 ] proved the four-color theorem with a computer check of more cases than any human could survey, mathematicians debated whether the theorem had been proved or merely shown to be true [ 39 ] . The proof came to be accepted in part because humans had designed its overall strategy and could understand both that strategy and the program that checked the cases; AI-generated proofs of the kind discussed in Section 3.3 may come with no human-understood strategy at all. The risk, then, is not that careless use of AI eliminates understanding at once, but that it erodes it gradually, until the community can no longer examine, take apart and contest the knowledge it relies on [ 34 ] . Nor is the principle tied to established methods: new practices, including AI-assisted ones, are consistent with it wherever they preserve or extend these capacities. 3 How: A Framework for Incorporating AI in Research Different research activities involve different kinds and levels of understanding and judgment. The principle yields a two-prong test that can be applied to each research activity to determine how AI can be incorporated in it without eroding the principle. The first three elements of the principle ground the first prong of the test; the fourth grounds the second. 1. Human understanding: delegate a task to AI only if the scientific community can still independently understand, defend and contest the resulting claims, and retain the skills to do so in the future. 2. Human direction: judgments about which questions matter and what findings mean for human ends remain with accountable humans: stakeholders for the goals, priorities and uses of research, and researchers, answerable to the scientific community, for the scientific process. We apply the test to the phases of research activities informed by and extending the Contributor Roles Taxonomy (CRediT), a standard used across disciplines and adopted by many publishers. The phases overlap and repeat, and the line between human and AI work runs within each phase rather than between them [ 40 ] , so the recommendations allocate roles inside each phase. Each subsection defines the phase, states our recommendation and then gives the argument for it, noting which prong it rests on. While the two-prong test states the requirements, the phase-specific recommendations here offer defeasible practices for meeting them. The evidence we cite concerns the effects of AI use on people, such as on skills and on the diversity of ideas, because these effects persist even if AI makes no errors. Scope and interpretation of the recommendations. This article focuses on the use of AI to partially or fully automate research tasks traditionally performed by humans. It does not primarily address the use of AI as a tutor to develop researchers’ knowledge and skills, although learning and research often overlap. Genuine human understanding can be acquired through AI-assisted processes, and automating research tasks does not always erode that understanding. What matters is whether the scientific community retains the capacity to comprehend, critically assess, and contest scientific claims, and to reproduce these capacities across generations. The recommendations below identify practices intended to safeguard these capacities and preserve human direction. They are not categorical restrictions on AI use; rather, they are default safeguards: practical ways of satisfying the two-prong test, to be adapted to the tasks, methods, and training needs of different scientific communities. Readers may reasonably disagree with particular defaults; such disagreements are best settled by applying the two-prong test to the case at hand, which is the standard the recommendations are meant to serve. The recommendations are addressed to the scientific community : researchers and the institutions that train, fund and evaluate them. Other actors now shape science as well, including the companies that build AI systems, and they are not bound by the community’s norms in the same way, even when their own researchers take part in it. Following these recommendations is therefore helpful but not sufficient to preserve human understanding and direction. The principle nonetheless offers a standard for judging other actors’ choices. Practices that support human understanding, such as releasing results openly with machine-checkable proofs and funding the community’s efforts to understand them, are consistent with it. Practices that impede it, such as releasing results faster than the community can examine them or in forms that cannot be independently reproduced, are not. Section 4 turns to some of the levers the scientific enterprise has over these conditions, including funding priorities and support for publicly governed models. 3.1 Conceptualization Conceptualization covers reviewing the literature, choosing a research question and generating hypotheses. Recommendation. AI may assist in generating candidate questions and hypotheses, but researchers should choose which to pursue, within the priorities stakeholders set. Authors should read and understand the work their choice of research question and subsequent claims rest on, and distinguish those references from ones they have only consulted. At any time a field faces many possible questions (there may be thousands of drug candidates to test), and AI can surface them faster than any human team. Choosing among them is a judgment about what we care about, which even a perfect model cannot settle on our behalf; this is the direction prong [ 4 , 9 ] . There is also a collective concern: if every researcher asks the same system which questions to pursue, the range of questions narrows. AI assistance makes ideas more similar to one another [ 41 , 42 ] and is associated with a narrower range of topics across science [ 13 ] , while collective understanding depends on diverse perspectives [ 5 ] and on a division of cognitive labor across competing approaches [ 43 , 44 ] . This narrowing is evidence about current AI tools, and more capable systems may be able to compensate for it, for example by deliberately varying assumptions and methods. The evidence is therefore a reason for caution now, and the recommendation itself rests on the direction prong. For the literature, the understanding prong implies that authors can defend only those claims that rest on work they have understood. Citing without reading predates AI [ 45 ] , but AI makes it easier. We therefore propose that papers distinguish core references , which the authors have read and understood, from skimmed references , which they have consulted, possibly with the help of AI. 3.2 Methodology Methodology is the choice and design of the method used to answer the research question. Recommendation. Researchers should choose their methods themselves. AI may propose candidate methods and critique the researchers’ choice, but a method should be adopted only once the researchers understand it well enough to judge whether it fits the problem. Early-career researchers should begin with their own search. Two reasons follow from the understanding prong. First, researchers can verify only methods they understand: a researcher who cannot program cannot faithfully check a simulation-based method, however plausible an AI makes it sound. Second, searching for a method is itself a way of learning about the phenomenon and of building skills for later problems, which matters most for early-career researchers. Learning an unfamiliar method with AI’s help is consistent with both reasons, as the scope note above allows, and an experienced researcher who asks AI for candidate methods loses little, provided they understand a method before adopting it. What the test rules out is adopting a method because an AI chose it: a researcher must understand a method before they can judge that it fits a particular research problem. 3.3 Investigation Investigation is the execution of the method: collecting data, running experiments, writing software and conducting formal analysis. Recommendation. How much of investigation can be delegated depends on where understanding resides in the method. In every field, early-career researchers should execute their methods without the aid of AI until they reach the appropriate level of competence. In a systematic review of a well-structured literature, understanding lies mainly in the synthesis rather than in the retrieval, so automating retrieval and screening passes the understanding prong. In ethnography, the relationship between researcher and participants is the method, so substituting AI changes the research itself, not only its speed. In every field, durability requires that new researchers acquire the skills to carry out and check the work. In one experiment, AI assistance while learning a new programming library impaired later conceptual understanding and debugging, without significant time savings ( [ 46 ] ; see also [ 47 ] ). A note on formal fields. Fields in which the work of investigation is itself formal or computational, such as mathematics, theoretical computer science and large-scale simulation studies, deserve particular attention, because their execution can be almost fully automated today. In October 2026, OpenAI publicly released a large set of new results in mathematics and theoretical computer science produced by an internal model, many accompanied by machine-checkable formalizations in the Lean proof language [ 48 ] . Formal verification can establish that such a proof is correct without any human grasping it, and even a mathematician who checks a proof line by line learns that the result holds rather than why. This falls short even of comprehension, the first dimension of understanding in Section 2.1 : it is closer to the testimony of a reliable source than to a grasp of the result [ 26 ] . Mathematicians have long held that the point of proof is human understanding rather than the certification of theorems [ 49 ] . The durability clause therefore requires that the community retain all three dimensions for such results: the capacity to explain them and identify their key ideas (comprehension), to critique them (critical assessment), and to reproduce the argument without the machine and extend its methods to new problems (capability retention). Verification, whether by a person or a proof checker, remains necessary, but it is where the work of human understanding begins, not where it ends. Scientific progress through AI-generated results. On a knowledge-based account of scientific progress [ 25 ] , each correct new theorem is progress. On the understanding-based account adopted here [ 6 ] , it is potential progress: the results advance human understanding once members of the community can explain, critique and build on them, and until then they resemble an archive of correct findings more than an addition to what the community understands. This does not diminish their value. It identifies the work that remains, and it explains why efforts to help mathematicians examine and understand AI-generated results matter as much as the results themselves. 3.4 Validation Validation is the authors’ own check that their results reproduce. Recommendation. AI can be used extensively for validation, including to find and fix errors, provided the researchers understand the work being checked and any fix that bears on their results. Early-career researchers should diagnose and fix errors themselves until they can do so competently. Checking that results reproduce does not by itself produce new understanding, so this is the phase in which the test permits the most delegation: formally verifying proofs the researchers wrote (for example, with Lean), generating test cases at scale in computational work, or checking that every quotation traces back to the original interview data. This presupposes that the understanding already exists. When the investigation itself was delegated to AI, as in the cases discussed in Section 3.3 , a successful check establishes that the result holds, not that anyone understands it. Fixing errors follows the same logic as investigation: what matters is where understanding resides. Many errors, such as a routine coding bug or a mislabeled axis, have no bearing on what researchers must understand to defend their claims, and AI can fix them. An error that changes a result is different: the researchers must understand what went wrong and why the fix is correct, or they can no longer defend the claim. Because diagnosing errors is also how researchers learn to avoid them, early-career researchers should do so themselves until they are competent. 3.5 Interpretation Interpretation is deciding what the results mean. Recommendation. To safeguard understanding, researchers should form their own interpretation first, consult AI for alternative readings only afterwards, and keep the final judgment. Interpretation is where understanding is formed. If AI interprets the results, the community holds testimony rather than understanding [ 26 ] , which fails the understanding prong. Deciding what a result means for human ends falls under the direction prong. The order matters even if the AI’s reading is correct, because seeing it first skips the work through which understanding is formed and anchors the researcher’s own reading [ 50 ] . 3.6 Writing Writing covers drafting the paper and then reviewing and editing it, including seeking feedback before submission. Recommendation. Authors should develop and document their own arguments before relying on AI. AI may then be used to elaborate on and polish an argument the authors have already worked out, provided they can defend every claim it adds, and to give feedback before the paper goes to colleagues. Under the understanding prong, documenting one’s argument is how authors work out and consolidate their ideas; by analogy, evidence from education shows that writing about content improves learning [ 51 ] . Elaborating on and polishing an argument the authors have already documented does not remove that understanding, and it serves the direction prong by lowering a barrier unrelated to the quality of the science: AI writing assistance is used disproportionately by researchers from non-English-speaking countries [ 52 ] . Fields in which argument and prose cannot be separated, such as philosophy, may reasonably restrict AI as a writing assistant. Feedback from AI before submission can catch clear errors and check conformity with a venue’s conventions, leaving human reviewers to focus on substance and on understanding the work. 3.7 Community evaluation Community evaluation is the assessment of work by others: peer review, post-publication critique and independent replication. Recommendation. Peer review and post-publication critique should remain human. AI can be used for independent replication. Under the understanding prong, peer review tests whether a contribution can be understood by other humans; under the direction prong, it tests whether the contribution matters to the community it addresses.
